rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A believer must not let Satan lure him back into the abyss from which God rescued him.
rows.anchor: must not be lured away by Satan and not plunge into the abyss from which the Almighty has saved them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic wording makes even the name of defiance after faith very evil; once faith is cherished, fisq itself should be abhorrent.
rows.anchor: very evil is the name of fisq after faith.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earlier prohibitions are forms of fisq, so believers should detest even its name; those who persist after clear warning are wronging themselves, not suffering divine injustice.
rows.anchor: whatever things have been prohibited in the previous verses are of the category of fisq

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who do not repent after the specified acts are warned that they are wrongdoers and bear responsibility after God has made faith and the consequences of fisq clear.
rows.anchor: people who do not repent on these things should remember that they are wrong-doers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address turns afresh to believers because seemingly small evils can damage the heart until it is no longer receptive to taqwā.
rows.anchor: Here the believers are addressed afresh and stopped

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thoughts shape social bonds, so Muslims should presume others well unless evidence defeats that presumption; when possible, seek a sound positive explanation, preferring a mistaken good opinion to a mistaken bad one.
rows.anchor: a Muslim must always think well of others unless it is proven to him that someone is not worthy of this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He compares obsessive suspicion to a hunter so intent on catching fish that he catches snakes too and may lose his own life.
rows.anchor: becomes so blind in his obsession for catching fish that he also catches snakes.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi cites a hadith description of the believer as noble and innocent; the note cites Abū Dā’ūd, Sunan 4790, without stating a grading.
rows.anchor: a believer is noble and innocent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The assumption that believers should treat others as enemies in political dealings conflicts with Qur’anic commands for humility toward believers and mercy among them.
rows.anchor: how can this political acumen be true for believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ban on probing targets inquisitiveness for evil ends: uncovering another person’s faults and private or family secrets, often from jealousy or hatred.
rows.anchor: the prohibition actually relates to being inquisitive for an evil purpose.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scandal-seeking journalism exemplifies spying to humiliate others: success is measured by finding private scandals that sell papers.
rows.anchor: the journalist who is considered to be the most successful is the one who is able to lay his hands on a scandal

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Inquiry to learn a neighbor’s needs so as to help, or a state’s collection of information needed to discharge its duties to citizens, is not the forbidden spying; neighborly inquiry can be virtuous and state inquiry a responsibility.
rows.anchor: Such spying is a very virtuous act on the part of a neighbour

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Backbiting is speaking of someone’s flaws in their absence, in a way that leaves the target unaware.
rows.anchor: Backbiting means speaking about the flaws of a person in his absence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Backbiting is kept within a circle of like-minded confidants who share the aim or at least will not sympathize with the person being targeted.
rows.anchor: In pursuance of keeping it secret, a backbiter gives his statements before people who hold the same opinion and are his confidants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The image equates backbiting with eating a dead, defenseless brother’s flesh; because no one accepts that horror, the verse asks why people commit its equivalent.
rows.anchor: speaks ill of his brother in his absence is as if he is eating his flesh while he is dead

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the corpse simile, maytan is an accusative of state (ḥāl) from the omitted genitive in akhīhi, depicting the brother’s helplessness.
rows.anchor: is an accusative of state from the muḍāf found in

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The command to fear God warns habitual backbiters that they may lose faith and urges repentance and self-reform, for God eagerly forgives and shows mercy to the penitent.
rows.anchor: those who become used to consuming the meat of their brother without any cost start cherishing this

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The six bans divide into three public wrongs and three private wrongs done in a person’s absence; both serve tazkiyah, linked to leaving hidden and open sin, and awareness that God sees the hidden grounds taqwā.
rows.anchor: the first of these three: making fun, defaming others and calling others by bad names are evils which a person commits openly

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The universal address uproots pride in lineage, family, and tribe: all humanity descends from Adam and Eve and no one is superior by species.
rows.anchor: they are the progeny of one man and woman: all mankind was created from Adam and Eve

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Families and tribes exist so people can identify one another, like distinctions of appearance, color, and physique; these divisions confer no further status.
rows.anchor: families and tribes so that people can recognize one another. It has no significance beyond this.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Honor before God depends on taqwā: the most honored is most mindful of Him and vigilant in observing His bounds.
rows.anchor: The basis of respect in the sight of God is taqwā.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows every person’s words and deeds and can honor an unknown person of low origin while casting an unworthy person from Quraysh or the Hashimites into the pit he deserves.
rows.anchor: He who is worthy of respect shall certainly gain a place of respect however unknown and of lowly origin he may be.

rows.speaker: some people
rows.claim: Some infer that Islam bars governments from investigating citizens’ private household affairs, limiting accountability to matters that come openly to notice; they cite a story about ʿUmar.
rows.anchor: some people think that just as Islam has stopped people from prying into the affairs of others, it has also stopped governments from prying

rows.speaker: ‘Umar (rta)
rows.claim: In the cited story, ʿUmar enters a house over its wall after hearing singing and finds wine and a woman; the resident accuses him of spying and entering unlawfully, and ʿUmar admits error, forgoes prosecution, and takes a promise of reform.
rows.anchor: ‘Umar (rta) acknowledged his mistake and did not proceed against that person

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islahi judges the story cited about ʿUmar unreliable both in its chain and in its content.
rows.anchor: neither is it reliable with regard to its chain of narration nor with regard to its content.
